questions.stem: Which is an example of asexual reproduction?
options: A strawberry plant producing new plants from its runners
A flower being pollinated by a bee carrying pollen
Two frogs releasing their sperm and eggs together into a pond
A seed forming after pollen fertilises an ovule
questions.explanation: Runners grow from the parent plant and root to form new plants by mitosis, so the offspring are genetically identical to the parent. Pollination, the release of sperm and eggs, and fertilisation of an ovule are all steps in sexual reproduction.

questions.stem: What is a biological advantage of asexual reproduction?
options: Harmful mutations are removed from the offspring by crossing over
A single individual can produce many offspring quickly, with no mate
The offspring vary, so some of them may survive a newly arrived disease
The offspring combine favourable alleles from two different parents
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction needs only one parent and no search for a mate, so populations can grow rapidly. Variation and the combining of alleles from two parents are advantages of sexual reproduction, and crossing over happens only in meiosis.

questions.stem: A plantation of genetically identical banana plants is grown from suckers. Why is the whole crop at risk?
options: Suckers carry only half of the parent's chromosomes, so the new plants are weaker
A disease that kills one plant can kill them all, because none has different alleles for resistance
The plants cannot produce fruit unless they are cross-pollinated by a different variety
The plants will mutate rapidly because they were produced asexually, and lose fruit quality
questions.explanation: Plants grown from suckers are clones, so if one is susceptible to a disease every plant is. A genetically varied crop would be more likely to include some resistant plants. Suckers form by mitosis and carry the parent's full set of chromosomes.

questions.stem: Yeast cells reproduce when a small outgrowth forms on the parent cell, grows and separates as a new cell. What is this process?
options: Spore formation
Budding
Binary fission
Fragmentation
questions.explanation: In budding, a new individual grows as an outgrowth of the parent and then breaks away, as in yeast and hydra. Binary fission splits a cell into two equal halves, and fragmentation is regrowth of whole organisms from broken pieces.

questions.stem: Female Komodo dragons kept in zoos without any males have produced offspring from unfertilised eggs. What form of reproduction is this?
options: Fragmentation
Vegetative propagation
Parthenogenesis
Budding
questions.explanation: Parthenogenesis is the development of offspring from an egg that has not been fertilised, a form of asexual reproduction seen in some reptiles, insects and fish. Budding and fragmentation produce offspring from body tissue rather than eggs, and vegetative propagation occurs in plants.

questions.stem: Under which conditions is asexual reproduction most advantageous to a species?
options: In a stable environment to which the parent is already well adapted
In a changing environment where new diseases keep appearing
When the population must adapt quickly to a newly arrived predator
When a small, isolated population already has very low genetic diversity
questions.explanation: Clones of a well-adapted parent will be well suited to an environment that does not change, and asexual reproduction lets them multiply quickly. Changing environments, new diseases and new predators favour the variation that sexual reproduction provides.

questions.stem: What is the main biological advantage of sexual reproduction?
options: It produces more offspring, more quickly and with less energy than asexual reproduction
It allows a single parent to produce offspring without needing to find a mate
It produces offspring identical to a parent that is already well adapted
It produces genetically varied offspring, so some may survive environmental change
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction mixes alleles from two parents, so offspring differ and a population is more likely to include individuals that survive a disease or change in conditions. It is usually slower and needs more energy than asexual reproduction, and it needs two parents.

questions.stem: Which three processes make the offspring of sexual reproduction genetically different from each other?
options: Crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation
Binary fission, budding and fragmentation of the parents
Mitosis, cytokinesis and DNA replication in the parents
Crossing over, mitosis and the cloning of each fertilised egg
questions.explanation: Crossing over and independent assortment in meiosis make each gamete different, and random fertilisation means any sperm can combine with any egg. Binary fission, budding, fragmentation and mitosis produce genetically identical cells.

questions.stem: Many aphids reproduce asexually throughout summer, then reproduce sexually in autumn, laying eggs that survive the winter. What is the most likely advantage of this strategy?
options: Sexual reproduction in autumn produces more offspring than asexual reproduction in summer
Rapid population growth while conditions are good, then varied offspring to face the harsher, changing season
Varied offspring while conditions are good, then rapid population growth when food is scarce in winter
Identical eggs survive winter better than varied eggs, because all are adapted in the same way
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction in summer lets the population multiply rapidly while food is plentiful and conditions are stable. Sexual reproduction before winter produces genetically varied eggs, improving the chance some survive the unpredictable conditions ahead. Sexually produced eggs are not identical, and sexual reproduction is the slower strategy.

questions.stem: Why is sexual reproduction considered costly compared with asexual reproduction, despite its advantages?
options: Every offspring inherits all the harmful mutations carried by both of its parents
Finding a mate takes time and energy, and only females bear young, so populations grow more slowly
Offspring are identical to their parents, so the variation in the population is gradually lost
Meiosis produces diploid gametes, which take twice as much energy to make as haploid cells
questions.explanation: In a sexual population only females produce offspring and individuals must find and attract mates, so the population grows more slowly than an asexual one where every individual reproduces. Sexual reproduction produces varied, not identical, offspring, and gametes made by meiosis are haploid.

questions.stem: In somatic cell nuclear transfer, what is placed into an egg cell that has had its nucleus removed?
options: The nucleus of a body cell from the animal to be cloned
A sperm cell taken from the animal to be cloned
Cells split from an early embryo of another animal
The mitochondria of a body cell from the animal to be cloned
questions.explanation: A nucleus from a somatic (body) cell of the animal to be copied is transferred into an enucleated egg, which is then stimulated to divide and implanted into a surrogate. Splitting early embryos is a different cloning technique, embryo splitting.

questions.stem: Dolly the sheep was cloned from the nucleus of an udder cell of a Finn Dorset ewe and an enucleated egg from a Scottish Blackface ewe, then carried by a Scottish Blackface surrogate. Whose nuclear DNA did Dolly have?
options: Half the Finn Dorset's and half the egg donor's
The Finn Dorset ewe that donated the udder cell
The Scottish Blackface ewe that donated the egg
The Scottish Blackface ewe that carried her
questions.explanation: All of Dolly's nuclear DNA came from the transferred udder cell nucleus, so she was a Finn Dorset, with its white face, unlike the Blackface ewes. The egg donor's nucleus had been removed, and the surrogate only provided the uterus.

questions.stem: A clone made by somatic cell nuclear transfer is not entirely genetically identical to the animal that donated the nucleus. Why not?
options: Crossing over happens in the nucleus as it is transferred into the egg
Half of its chromosomes come from the surrogate mother that carries it
The electrical pulse used to fuse the cells changes some of its genes
Its mitochondrial DNA comes from the cytoplasm of the donated egg cell
questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry their own DNA, and the clone's mitochondria come from the egg, which had its nucleus removed but kept its cytoplasm. Crossing over happens only in meiosis, and the surrogate contributes no DNA.

questions.stem: In embryo splitting, the cells of an early embryo are separated and each grows into an animal. Which statement about these animals is correct?
options: They are clones of the father, who provided the sperm
They are all genetically different, like normal siblings
They are clones of each other, but not of either parent
They are clones of the mother, who provided the egg
questions.explanation: The embryo formed from one egg and one sperm, so it is a genetic mix of both parents. Its cells are identical to each other, so the animals grown from them are clones of each other, like identical twins, but not of either parent.

questions.stem: Why might a farmer clone a prize dairy cow by somatic cell nuclear transfer rather than breed from her sexually?
options: The clone is more genetically diverse than her, so it resists more diseases
Cloning combines the best alleles of the cow and of a prize bull in one calf
Cloning adds new alleles for higher milk yield to the clone's genome
The clone has her exact combination of alleles, which sexual reproduction would shuffle
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction mixes the cow's alleles with a bull's and shuffles them in meiosis, so offspring may not inherit her valuable combination. A clone receives her whole nuclear genome. Cloning adds no diversity and no new alleles.

questions.stem: A conservation program considers cloning the last few surviving individuals of an endangered species. What is the main biological limitation of this plan?
options: Cloning adds no new genetic diversity, so the population stays vulnerable to disease
Cloned animals are always infertile, so they could never breed with one another
Cloning works only for plants, so it cannot be used for endangered animals
Cloned animals always die young, before they are old enough to reproduce
questions.explanation: Clones only copy existing genomes, so a cloned population has no more genetic diversity than the few survivors. Cloned mammals can be fertile and have had healthy offspring; Dolly herself gave birth to lambs. Many animal species have now been cloned.

questions.stem: Which technique is used to clone plants?
options: Fertilising an ovule with pollen by hand
Growing new plants from stem cuttings
Cross-pollinating two plant varieties
Collecting seed from open-pollinated flowers
questions.explanation: A cutting grows into a new plant by mitosis, so it is genetically identical to the parent; tissue culture and grafting also clone plants. Pollination and fertilisation of ovules are sexual reproduction, producing seeds that differ genetically.

questions.stem: Why is genetic diversity within a population important for its survival?
options: It makes individuals more alike, so they all respond to change the same way
It stops new mutations from arising and spreading through the population
It increases the chance that some individuals have alleles to survive a change
It ensures that every individual in it is resistant to every disease it meets
questions.explanation: A diverse gene pool means individuals differ in their traits, so when a disease or environmental change arrives some are likely to survive and reproduce. No population is resistant to everything, and diversity makes individuals less alike, not more.

questions.stem: What is a population's gene pool?
options: All the individuals of one species in an area
All the dominant alleles carried in the population
All the alleles of all the genes in the population
All the genes in the genome of one individual
questions.explanation: The gene pool is the total set of alleles carried by all members of a population. One individual's genes make up its genome, and the individuals themselves make up the population.

questions.stem: A new viral disease reaches two populations of the same species. Population A has high genetic diversity and population B has very low genetic diversity. What is the most likely outcome?
options: Both populations will lose the same proportion, because they are the same species
Population B is more likely to survive, because uniform individuals share resistance
Population B is more likely to suffer heavy losses, because its individuals respond alike
Population A is more likely to suffer heavy losses, because it has more alleles to lose
questions.explanation: In a population with little diversity, if one individual is susceptible most others are too, so the disease can sweep through it. A diverse population is more likely to contain resistant individuals that survive and reproduce. Uniformity only helps if the shared alleles happen to give resistance, which cannot be relied on.

questions.stem: Conservation managers move a few animals from a large population into a small, isolated population of the same species. What is the main purpose?
options: To introduce new alleles and increase the small population's genetic diversity
To make the small population genetically uniform so that it breeds true
To reduce the number of different alleles present in the small, isolated population
To replace the small population with animals that are clones of each other
questions.explanation: Small, isolated populations lose alleles and suffer from inbreeding. Bringing in individuals from elsewhere adds alleles to the gene pool, increasing diversity and the population's ability to cope with change. Uniformity and fewer alleles are the problem being fixed.

questions.stem: What is a structural adaptation?
options: An action that an organism carries out that aids its survival
A change an individual develops during its life to cope with conditions
A physical feature of an organism's body that aids its survival
An internal body process of an organism that aids its survival
questions.explanation: Structural adaptations are physical features such as thick fur, spines or sunken stomata. Internal processes are physiological adaptations and actions are behavioural adaptations. Adaptations are inherited, so a change acquired during one individual's life is not an adaptation.

questions.stem: On hot days red kangaroos lick their forearms, and the evaporating saliva cools blood flowing close to the skin. What type of adaptation is the licking?
options: Physiological
Acquired
Behavioural
Structural
questions.explanation: Licking is something the kangaroo does, so it is a behavioural adaptation. The network of blood vessels near the skin of the forearms is a structural feature, but the question asks about the licking itself.

questions.stem: The spinifex hopping mouse of arid central Australia produces extremely concentrated urine. What type of adaptation is this?
options: Acquired
Physiological
Structural
Behavioural
questions.explanation: Producing concentrated urine is an internal body function, carried out by the kidneys, which makes it a physiological adaptation. It conserves water in an environment where little is available to drink.

questions.stem: A seal has a thick layer of blubber, reduces blood flow to its flippers in icy water, and hauls out onto rocks to bask in the sun. What type of adaptation is each feature, in that order?
options: Structural; physiological; behavioural
Physiological; structural; behavioural
Structural; behavioural; physiological
Behavioural; physiological; structural
questions.explanation: Blubber is a physical feature of the body, so it is structural. Reducing blood flow is an internal process controlled by the body, so it is physiological. Hauling out to bask is an action, so it is behavioural.

questions.stem: A person who moves from the coast to a high-altitude town makes more red blood cells over the following weeks. Why is this not an adaptation in the biological sense?
options: It happens over weeks, and adaptations must happen within seconds of a change
It is a change within one person's life, not an inherited trait shared by the population
It is a physiological change, and only structural features count as adaptations
It improves the person's survival, and adaptations do not affect survival
questions.explanation: Biological adaptations are inherited features that have become common in a population because they aided survival and reproduction. Adjusting to altitude during one lifetime is acclimatisation and is not passed on. Physiological features can be adaptations, as concentrated urine in desert mammals shows.

questions.stem: The leaves of many eucalypts hang vertically. How does this help them survive in hot, dry conditions?
options: Water drains to the leaf tip, where the stomata absorb it from the surface
The stomata face the ground, so the leaves take in more carbon dioxide
Less leaf surface faces the midday sun, reducing heating and water loss
More leaf surface faces the midday sun, increasing photosynthesis and cooling
questions.explanation: A vertical leaf presents only its edge to the high midday sun, so it absorbs less heat and loses less water. Facing more surface to the sun would raise leaf temperature and transpiration. Stomata release water vapour; they do not absorb liquid water from the leaf surface.

questions.stem: Which feature would most reduce water loss in a plant of an arid environment?
options: A thin cuticle that lets more light reach the mesophyll
Large, flat leaves with many stomata on their upper surface
Sunken stomata surrounded by hairs that trap humid air
Stomata raised on bumps where air moves freely past them
questions.explanation: Sunken stomata and hairs hold a layer of still, humid air over the pores, reducing the gradient for water vapour to diffuse out. Raised stomata in moving air, thin cuticles and large leaves with many exposed stomata all increase water loss.

questions.stem: Water lilies have their stomata on the upper surface of their floating leaves, unlike most land plants. Why is this an adaptation?
options: The upper surface is shaded by the water, so stomata there lose less water vapour
Water must enter the leaf through the stomata to keep the leaf floating on the pond
The lower surface is too warm, so carbon dioxide cannot dissolve in the mesophyll
The lower surface touches the water, so gas exchange with the air must happen on top
questions.explanation: Stomata exchange gases with the air, and the underside of a floating leaf is in water, so stomata there would be useless. Water conservation is not a problem for a plant surrounded by water, so the upper surface's exposure to the sun is not a disadvantage.

questions.stem: The arctic fox has small ears and short legs, while the fennec fox of the Sahara has very large ears. How do the arctic fox's features help it survive?
options: A lower surface area to volume ratio reduces heat loss to the cold air
A higher surface area to volume ratio reduces heat loss to the cold air
A lower surface area to volume ratio increases heat gain from the sun
A higher surface area to volume ratio lets its fur trap more warm air
questions.explanation: Small ears and short legs reduce the body's surface area relative to its volume, so less heat is lost to cold surroundings. The fennec fox's large ears do the opposite, increasing surface area to lose heat in a hot desert.

questions.stem: Some archaea live in hot springs at temperatures that would kill most organisms. Which adaptation makes this possible?
options: Moving to cooler water each day to escape the hottest periods
Enzymes and other proteins that keep their shape at high temperatures
Cell walls that stop any heat from entering the cell's cytoplasm
A complete lack of enzymes, so there is nothing in the cell that heat can denature
questions.explanation: Heat normally denatures proteins, but these organisms have enzymes whose structure stays stable at high temperature. All living cells need enzymes, and no cell wall can keep heat out of a cell sitting in hot water.

questions.stem: What is a keystone species?
options: A species found naturally in only one ecosystem in the world
A species whose effect on its ecosystem is much greater than its abundance suggests
The most abundant species in an ecosystem, making up most of its biomass
A producer found at the base of every food chain in an ecosystem, such as a grass
questions.explanation: Like the keystone of an arch, a keystone species holds its community together, and removing it causes large changes even though it may be uncommon. The most abundant species is not necessarily a keystone, and a species found in only one place is endemic.

questions.stem: Along parts of the Pacific coast of North America, sea otters eat sea urchins, which graze on kelp. What happened to kelp forests where sea otters were hunted out?
options: Urchin numbers fell, and the kelp forests grew denser than before
Urchin numbers rose, and the kelp forests grew denser than before
Urchin numbers fell, and the kelp forests were overgrazed and declined
Urchin numbers rose, and the kelp forests were overgrazed and declined
questions.explanation: Without otters eating them, urchin populations grew and grazed the kelp heavily, turning forests into bare areas known as urchin barrens. The otter's effect reaches two feeding levels down, which is why it is called a keystone species.

questions.stem: Sea stars on a rocky shore eat mussels, which can outcompete other attached species for space on the rock. If the sea stars are removed, what is the most likely change?
options: Mussels spread over the rock, and the number of species on the shore rises
Mussels decline, and the other attached species decline with them
Mussels spread over the rock, and the number of species on the shore falls
Mussels decline, and the number of species on the shore rises
questions.explanation: Predation by sea stars keeps the dominant competitor in check, leaving space for other species. With the predator gone, mussels take over the rock and crowd other species out, so diversity falls. Removing a predator of mussels lets them increase, not decline.

questions.stem: A top predator is removed from a fenced reserve. Over ten years a smaller predator increases in number and populations of small ground-dwelling mammals fall. Which chain of events best explains this?
options: Top predator removed → smaller predator decreases → less predation on small mammals
Top predator removed → small mammals increase → smaller predator runs short of food
Top predator removed → smaller predator increases → less predation on small mammals
Top predator removed → smaller predator increases → more predation on small mammals
questions.explanation: The top predator had kept the smaller predator in check. Freed from that control, the smaller predator increased and ate more small mammals, which declined. This release of a mid-level predator shows how top predators shape the size of populations they do not eat directly.

questions.stem: How can a top predator influence the distribution of its prey, not just their numbers?
options: Prey avoid areas where the risk of predation is high, so they gather in safer habitats
Prey gather in areas where predators are most common, because the food is richest there
Prey spread out evenly across every habitat, regardless of where predators hunt them
Prey stop moving between habitats, so the predator cannot change where they are found
questions.explanation: Prey often change where they feed and shelter to avoid predators, so a predator changes the distribution and density of prey across an ecosystem as well as their total numbers. This in turn affects which plants are grazed and where.

questions.stem: In a classic predator–prey cycle, how do peaks in the predator population relate to peaks in the prey population?
options: Predator numbers stay level as prey numbers cycle
Predator peaks come shortly after prey peaks
Predator peaks come shortly before prey peaks
Predator and prey peaks happen at the same time
questions.explanation: Plentiful prey lets predators breed and increase, so predator numbers peak after the prey peak. As predators increase they reduce prey, and then predators decline from lack of food. The lag means the predator peak follows the prey peak.

questions.stem: Ecologists count 120 bilbies in a 40 hectare fenced reserve. What is the population density?
options: 4800 bilbies per hectare
80 bilbies per hectare
3 bilbies per hectare
0.33 bilbies per hectare
questions.explanation: Population density is the number of individuals per unit area: 120 ÷ 40 = 3 bilbies per hectare. Dividing the area by the number gives 0.33, and multiplying gives 4800.

questions.stem: Seedlings of a shrub grow in tight groups around their parent plants, because the seeds fall close by. What distribution pattern does this population show?
options: Linear, with individuals in long single rows
Clumped, with individuals gathered in groups
Uniform, with individuals evenly spaced
Random, with no pattern to the spacing
questions.explanation: Individuals gathered in groups show a clumped distribution, common where seeds fall near the parent or resources are patchy. Uniform distribution has individuals evenly spaced, often because of competition, and random distribution shows no pattern.

questions.stem: Ants live in the hollow thorns of an acacia tree and attack animals that try to eat its leaves, while the tree provides the ants with food and shelter. What kind of relationship is this?
options: Commensalism
Parasitism
Competition
Mutualism
questions.explanation: Both species benefit, the ants gaining food and shelter and the tree gaining protection, which is mutualism. In commensalism only one species benefits and the other is unaffected, and in parasitism one benefits at the other's expense.

questions.stem: Two bird species on an island both eat seeds of the same size, which are in limited supply. What interaction is this?
options: Commensalism
Interspecific competition
Intraspecific competition
Mutualism
questions.explanation: Competition between different species for the same limited resource is interspecific competition. Intraspecific competition is between members of the same species. Neither species benefits from the other's presence, so it is not mutualism or commensalism.
